name: Rider–Waite Tarot
subtitle: The Rider–Waite–Smith tradition
about: Seventy-eight cards: twenty-two Major Arcana for life’s great passages, and four suits (Wands, Cups, Swords and Pentacles) for its everyday weather. Each card can come upright or reversed, showing its light or its shadow side.
history: Tarot began as a card game in 15th-century Italy and became a tool for reflection in 18th-century France. The Rider–Waite–Smith deck, drawn by Pamela Colman Smith to A. E. Waite’s design and published in 1909, gave every card a picture, and its imagery still shapes most tarot today.

name: Catholic Saints
subtitle: A deck of holy companions
about: Sixty holy companions of the Catholic tradition: apostles and martyrs, mystics and scholars, servants of the poor, and the three archangels. Each card offers a message for your question through a saint’s virtue, upright or reversed, with their feast day.
history: The Church has kept the memory of the saints since the earliest martyrs, and devotional holy cards have carried their images into homes and prayer books since the 1400s. This deck continues that tradition: each saint is remembered on their feast day, when their card comes dressed for the feast.

name: Zodiac & Astrology
subtitle: Signs, planets, houses and the moon
about: The whole sky in one deck: the twelve signs, the planets, the twelve houses, the phases of the moon, the four elements and the lunar nodes. Each card offers a message for your question through one part of the sky, upright or reversed.
history: Astrology’s language of signs and houses grew from Babylonian sky-watching through Hellenistic Egypt, Greece and the medieval world. Its symbols have been read as a mirror for the inner life for more than two thousand years.

name: Archetypes
subtitle: The patterns we live by
about: The Innocent, the Hero, the Caregiver, the Sage: the recurring characters that shape stories and lives. Each card offers a message for your question through an archetype you might be living, resisting or growing into, upright or reversed.
history: The idea of universal patterns of character runs from ancient myth through Carl Jung’s archetypes to modern storytelling and personality work. This deck gathers the best known of them into a single circle.

name: Jungian Psychology
subtitle: Symbols of the inner life
about: The Shadow, the Persona, the Self, synchronicity and the language of dreams. Each card offers a message for your question through the ideas of depth psychology, upright or reversed.
history: Carl Gustav Jung (1875–1961) explored the unconscious through dreams, myth, alchemy and art. His ideas, including the shadow, the anima and animus, individuation and synchronicity, still shape how many people reflect on their inner lives.

cards.name: Dissolution

name: Hindu Deities
subtitle: Faces of the divine
about: Ganesha who clears the way, Lakshmi of abundance, Saraswati of wisdom, Shiva in stillness and the avatars of Vishnu. Each card offers a message for your question through the quality a deity embodies, upright or reversed.
history: The deities on these cards come from the Vedas, the epics (the Ramayana and the Mahabharata) and the Puranas, and are honoured across India and the world in temples, homes and festivals.

expansions.name: Sacred Presence
expansions.subtitle: The Mahavidyas, the forms of Durga and the gods’ companions

name: Dream Archetypes
subtitle: The places and scenes of our dreams
about: The childhood home, the endless staircase, the locked door, the deep water: the scenes that return in dreams across lives and cultures. Each card offers a message for your question through one of them, upright or reversed.
history: People have kept and read their dreams since the clay tablets of Mesopotamia and the dream books of ancient Egypt. In the twentieth century Freud and Jung turned to dreams as a language of the inner life, and the scenes on these cards are among the ones most often recorded.

name: Animal Symbolism
subtitle: What the animals have long stood for
about: The wolf, the heron, the honey bee and the great horned owl: forty animals and the qualities people have long seen in them. Each card offers a message for your question through an animal’s spirit meaning, upright or reversed. Three expansions add the creatures of the desert, the woodlands and the high country.
history: Animals carry meaning in nearly every culture’s stories, from fables and heraldry to the medieval bestiaries and the folklore of the places they live. This deck draws on that long habit of looking to animals for something of ourselves.

name: Crystals & Stones
subtitle: The lore of stones
about: Amethyst, labradorite, rose quartz and obsidian: thirty-six stones and the qualities their lore has given them. Each card offers a message for your question through a stone’s meaning in crystal lore, upright or reversed.
history: Stones have been carried, worn and given meaning for thousands of years, from the engraved gems of the ancient world to the medieval lapidaries that described each stone’s virtues. This deck keeps to that symbolic tradition.

expansions.name: Hidden Treasures
expansions.subtitle: Eighteen rarer stones and their lore

name: Angels & Sacred Messengers
subtitle: Archangels, guardians and holy messengers
about: Michael, Gabriel and Raphael, the guardian angel, the seraphim and the white feather: forty cards from the long tradition of heavenly messengers. Each card offers a message for your question through a messenger’s spiritual meaning, upright or reversed.
history: Angels appear as messengers in the Hebrew Bible, the New Testament and the Qur’an. Later writers ordered them into choirs of seraphim, cherubim and thrones, and names such as Uriel, Raziel and Metatron come from Jewish and Christian writings and devotional traditions that followed.

name: Inner Alchemist
subtitle: The stages of inner transformation
about: Calcination, dissolution, the crucible and the philosopher’s stone: the stages of the alchemists’ Great Work, read as stages of inner change. Each card offers a message for your question through a moment in the slow work of becoming, upright or reversed.
history: European alchemists described their Great Work as a sequence of burning, dissolving, separating and joining. Carl Jung later read their texts as a map of psychological transformation, and this deck follows that reading.

name: The Language of Flowers
subtitle: What flowers have long been said to mean
about: The rose, the forget-me-not, the snowdrop and the lotus: thirty-six flowers and the meanings people have given them. Each card offers a message for your question through a flower’s symbolic meaning, upright or reversed.
history: Flowers have carried meaning across many cultures. In the 1800s it became a fashion in Britain and America, where dictionaries of floriography let a bouquet speak for the giver; the lotus, chrysanthemum and cherry blossom bring meanings from Asian traditions too.

name: Love & Connection
subtitle: The ways we love and are loved
about: Trust, tenderness, repair and boundaries: thirty-seven cards on the qualities that let love grow, between partners, friends and family, and toward yourself. Each card offers a message for your question, upright or reversed.
history: Every tradition has had words for love’s many forms, from the Greeks’ eros, philia and agape onward. This deck draws on that long reflection, and on what people have learned about how close relationships are kept and mended.

name: Shadow Garden
subtitle: Tending what grows in the dark
about: The mask, the inner critic, the bitter root and the night bloom: thirty-six cards for the parts of ourselves we hide or avoid, met gently, the way a gardener tends what grows in the dark. Each card offers a message for your question, upright or reversed.
history: Carl Jung called the hidden and disowned parts of the self the shadow, and saw meeting them as part of becoming whole. Shadow work carries that idea into reflection and journaling; this deck gives each part a place in the garden.
